acceptance_criteria.criterion: store init creates ~/.ai-insights/stores.json with the current ledger root as the default store
store add test-store /tmp/test-store registers the store and creates an empty .repositories.json in /tmp/test-store
store repo add my-repo test-store writes a repository entry to test-store's .repositories.json
store list displays all stores with their repository and project counts
store conflicts shows repos registered in multiple stores with winner/shadowed indicators
store default <id> updates the default_store field in stores.json

summary: FAIL — storeRepoMove() validates after mutation. The source registry is written to disk (repo removed) inside the search loop before the function checks for a duplicate in the target store. In a conflict scenario (repo in both stores), this produces: source mutated unexpectedly + ok:false return. The fix requires moving the target-duplicate check before the source removal loop. All 6 ACs pass; all other store commands (storeInit, storeAdd, storeRemove, storeList, storeSetDefault, storeConflicts, storeRepoAdd, storeRepoList) are correct and well-tested.

comments.note: Non-blocking: saveConfig() calls mkdirSync(join(homedir(), AI_INSIGHTS_DIR)) unconditionally even when a test-override configPath is provided. Since mkdirSync with recursive:true is idempotent and only creates a directory (no file written to homedir), this is safe but reduces test isolation purity. A _storesDirOverride param on saveConfig (and storeInit) would make these fully hermetic. Already flagged by Developer and QA — noting here for completeness.

Overall store-commands.js architecture is well-structured: pure-JS compatible with TypeScript schemas, cross-platform (path.join/resolve throughout, shell:false in spawnSync), comprehensive JSDoc, and good separation between I/O helpers and command functions. The storeRepoMove ordering bug is the sole blocking issue — all other commands are correct.

comments.note: saveConfig() unconditionally calls mkdirSync(join(homedir(), AI_INSIGHTS_DIR)) even when a test-override configPath is provided, touching the real user filesystem during tests. This has now been flagged by Developer, QA, and the previous Reviewer across multiple pipeline passes — it's clearly a known limitation and is idempotent/harmless. Formally noting it here as the third observation so it can be addressed as a standalone improvement WP. A _storesDirOverride parameter on saveConfig() and storeInit() would make both fully hermetic without breaking the production code path.

cmdStore's list, conflicts, and status cases each have an if (!result.ok) guard that is unreachable: storeList(), storeConflicts(), and storeStatus() always return ok: true (returning empty arrays on missing config, not ok: false). The defensive guards are harmless, but they're dead code. If these functions are ever extended to signal partial failures, the ok: false path would become reachable. Noting for completeness — not blocking, and the pattern is consistent across other command handlers in cli.js.

storeRemove() when removing the last store leaves default_store pointing to the deleted store ID (config has stores: [] but default_store: 'deleted-id'). The condition config.stores.length > 0 gates the default_store reassignment. In practice all consumers (storeList, storeConflicts, storeSetDefault) handle the empty-stores case gracefully and return early, so this is never surfaced. Still, it leaves the config in a technically inconsistent state. A defensive null-out (config.default_store = null) when stores becomes empty would make the invariant cleaner.

[documentation-forward] scripts/lib/store-commands.js exports several internal I/O helpers — resolveConfigPath, expandPath, registryPath, loadConfig, saveConfig, loadRegistry, saveRegistry — alongside the primary command functions. These are consumed by tests but there is no documentation distinguishing them from the public command API. Adding a JSDoc comment block at the module level (or a brief section header comment) that delineates the public command functions from the exported-for-testing I/O helpers would help future maintainers understand the intended consumption surface.

readJsonSync catches all errors silently (bare catch {} returning null). This is intentional and consistent with the TypeScript loadRegistry behavior, but it means permissions errors, disk-full events, and malformed JSON all surface as the same empty-result state. For a CLI tool this is fine. If the module grows to support production workflows where silent-null is ambiguous, a structured error return (ok: false with a reason) would be worth considering.
